The Cost of Coordination

Why every organization eventually becomes a meeting about meetings

Karina Vols · April 2, 2026

Every organization, given enough time, converges on a fixed point: a meeting whose only purpose is to schedule another meeting. This is not a moral failing. It is a thermodynamic one. As the number of people who must agree before anything can move grows, the cost of coordination grows faster than the work the coordination is supposed to enable. Eventually it consumes the whole budget.

The classical answer is decentralization. Push decisions to the edges; let small teams move fast; trust people. This works for a while, and then it doesn't, because the edges discover they cannot solve their problems alone. They need the other teams' help, the other teams' data, the other teams' attention. The cost of finding out what the other teams know becomes the new coordination tax.

The second-classical answer is process. Documents, RFCs, asynchronous review. This is better. It defers the cost across time rather than collapsing it into a meeting. But process has its own inflation: every new rule was once a bug fix, and the rules accumulate even after the bugs are gone. Five years in, you are following procedures whose original purpose nobody remembers.

I do not have a clean answer. The cleanest I have is this: coordination cost is the dual of trust. Where there is no trust, every micro-decision must be coordinated. Where there is high trust, only the load-bearing decisions need it. The work, then, is not to eliminate coordination; it is to spend trust where it earns the highest return.

That requires noticing trust, which most organizations are bad at, because trust is invisible until it is gone.

— K.V.
